latin.380: §. V. Enimverò sunt, tàm ex Reformatis Franciscus Burmannus, Synops. Theol. Tom. 2. p. 401. quàm ex Lutheranis, Joh. Wilhelm. Bajerus, Theol. Histor. p. 593. qui illo tempore PASCHASIUM RHADEBERTUM, Abbatem Corbeiensem, Bertrami adversarium Coævum, in libro ejusdem cum Bertrami libro nominis, primum Consubstantiationis Autorem Patremque constituunt.
latin.381: Rectiùs multo à Bellarmino Conversionis, Transsubstantiationis rudimenti, Propagatorem habitum, cùm Tom. Controv. de Eucharist. p. m. 579. tùm in libro de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis p. 150., probante idem calculumque adjiciente suum Nostrate Viro Celeberrimo Wilhelmo Caveô, Script. Eccles. Hist. literaria p. 376., suffulciendo hac in parte ipsis Rhadeberti enunciatis quàm plurimis in libro de corpore & sanguine Domini cap. 20.
latin.382: Et tantùm non extra dubium idem ponente Bertramô, quando duarum duntaxat, tempore suo, de praesentia corporis Christi in sacra Coena, sententiarum meminit, initio libri sui pag. m. 3. 55. quarum alteram, de Spirituali praesentia, ipsemet, cum Patribus omnium seculorum, fovet, alteram, de Corporali, per Conversionem panis, adductam, in Paschasio Rhadeberto, oppugnat; Tertiam, si quae fuisset novitiamque, silentio haud praetervecturus, praesertim apud adversarium reperiundam.
latin.383: Quanquam interea illud allegato Bajero concedendum sit Paschasium Rhadebertum, primum fuisse, qui propriè dictum Corpus Christi, in S. Coena, Ore corporis, accipi docuerit, & quidem citra lacerationem, dentibus instituendam, libro de corpore & sanguine Christi cap. 4. restricta tamen etiam Orali acceptione ad solos fideles, lib. eodem cap. 6., cibum istum (nempe carnem Christi) non nisi solis amicis & fratribus Christi porrigi, disertis verbis cap. 10. professus.
latin.384: Quemadmodum similiter Burmanno largiendum, docuisse Rhadebertum, Carnem Christi etiam spiritualiter manducari in Sacramento Coenae, & sanguinem spiritualiter potari, cap. 5. 6. 10. 20.

pass_a.380: §. V. There are indeed, both from the Reformed Francis Burmann (Synopsis of Theology Tom. 2 p. 401) and from the Lutherans Joh. Wilhelm Bayer (Historical Theology p. 593), who at that time constitute PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, Abbot of Corbie, Bertram’s coeval adversary, in a book of the same name as Bertram’s book, the first Author and Father of Consubstantiation.
pass_a.381: Much more rightly held by Bellarmine to be a Propagator of Conversion, the rudiment of Transubstantiation — both in the Controversies Tom. on the Eucharist p. m. 579 and in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers p. 150 — our most celebrated countryman William Cave approving the same and adding his vote (Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers p. 376), this part being propped by Paschasius’s own very many utterances in On the body and blood of the Lord ch. 20.
pass_a.382: And Bertram nearly puts the same beyond doubt when at the start of his book (pp. m. 3, 55) he remembers only two opinions in his time on the presence of Christ’s body in the sacred Supper — of which the one, on Spiritual presence, he himself fosters with the Fathers of all ages; the other, on Corporal [presence] brought in by Conversion of the bread, he fights in Paschasius Radbertus; a Third, if there had been a novel one, he would hardly have passed in silence, especially one to be found in his adversary.
pass_a.383: Although meanwhile this is to be conceded to Bayer as alleged: that Paschasius Radbertus was the first who taught that the properly so-called Body of Christ is received in the Sacred Supper with the mouth of the body — and indeed without laceration to be done by the teeth (On the body and blood of Christ ch. 4) — yet with oral reception also restricted to the faithful alone (same book ch. 6), having professed in express words (ch. 10) that that food (namely Christ’s flesh) is offered only to Christ’s friends and brothers alone.
pass_a.384: Just as likewise it is to be granted to Burmann that Radbertus taught Christ’s Flesh is also eaten spiritually in the Sacrament of the Supper, and the blood drunk spiritually (chs. 5, 6, 10, 20).

380: §.V: Reformed Burmann (Synopsis Theol. II p. 401) and Lutheran Bayer (Theol. Histor. p. 593) both cast Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie — Bertram’s coeval adversary — as Consubstantiation’s first author and father.
They point to his book under the same title as Bertram’s.
381: Bellarmine is nearer the mark: Paschasius propagates Conversion, the seed of Transubstantiation (Eucharist Controversies; Ecclesiastical Writers).
Cave adds his vote; Paschasius’s own On the body and blood of the Lord ch. 20 props that reading.
382: Bertram nearly settles it: in his day he knows only two opinions — spiritual presence (his own, with the Fathers of every age) versus corporal presence by conversion of the bread (Paschasius), which he attacks.
Had there been a novel third (consubstantiation), he would not have passed it in silence — least of all in his adversary.
383: Concede to Bayer this much: Paschasius is first to teach oral reception of Christ’s proper body in the Supper without tooth-laceration.
Even then he restricts oral reception to the faithful alone — that food only for Christ’s friends and brothers.
384: Concede to Burmann likewise: Radbertus also teaches spiritual eating of the flesh and spiritual drinking of the blood in the Supper sacrament.
Stop before Berengar’s confuters as inventors of crassior/subtilior (Rupert of Deutz &c.).
